newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean president's son faces arrest - report.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean president's son faces arrest - report.

text.p: South Korean state prosecutors will seek the arrest of President Kim Young-sam's son, but not in connection with a loans-for-kickbacks scandal, the chief prosecutor was quoted as saying on Tuesday.

Prosecutor-general Kim Ki-soo told the Dong-A Ilbo daily that an investigation had found no evidence that Kim Hyun-chul committed any crime linked to the collapse in January of Hanbo Steel Co under $5.8 billion in debts.
But prosecutors said they would seek to arrest him on other charges unrelated to the loans scandal.
"We can't help but arrest Hyun-chul over personal irregularities unrelated to the Hanbo case because otherwise there might be accusations that we have tried to curtail the investigation," he said.
"The prosecution plans to arrest Mr Kim Hyun-chul before May 10 and effectively end the probe into the Hanbo loans case and suspicions over irregularities surrounding Hyun-chul."
There was no immediate explanation for the May 10 deadline, and prosecutors were not immediately available to comment on the report.
Prosecutors have been probing rumours that Kim Hyun-chul pocketed 200 billion won ($224 million) through a businessman, Park Tae-joong, acting as an agent for Hanbo.
Park was summoned for questioning on Monday and on Tuesday had still not emerged from the state prosecutors' office.
The chief prosecutor said Kim Hyun-chul had been "targeted for arrest", without giving details. He added he would take "moral responsibility" for the plan to seize the president's second son.
The collapse of South Korea's second largest steelmaker uncovered a web of corruption among politicians, bankers and businessmen.

Eleven people, including ruling and opposition party lawmakers, top aides to President Kim, bankers and Hanbo founder Chung Tae-soo are on trial for bribery. But the opposition has accused Kim Hyun-chul of being the key player.
In tearful testimony to parliament on Friday, Kim Hyun-chul begged for forgiveness for hurting his father but denied taking bribes to keep loans rolling in to Hanbo.
Public opinion polls indicate most Korean do not believe him and want legal action.

During the testimony, the junior Kim also countered charges by opposition politicians that he meddled in state affairs, including key appointments, and schemed with the help of the intelligence agencies.
Police said meanwhile they had determined that a former banker embroiled in the scandal and found hanging in his home on Monday committed suicide.
Park Suk-tae was an executive director of Korea First Bank, the main creditor of Hanbo Steel.
A police officer said the banker left a suicide note apologising to his former collegues and his family and asking that his body be cremated.
He was not charged with any crime but complained he felt humiliated by being called to testify before parliament on April 17 into the Hanbo failure, the officer said.
Park quit the bank in March after he was warned by the Office of Bank Supervision that the bank's loans to Hanbo were not backed by sufficient collateral, a bank spokesman said.
